original_claim: $500M–$700M annual direct fraud loss (US + Canada) from cargo identity-theft / double-brokering fraud
refined_claim: Cargo identity-theft and double-brokering fraud across the US and Canada caused estimated direct losses of approximately $330M (2023) to $455M (2024), per Verisk CargoNet’s annual actuarial tracking of US+Canada incidents (Tier 3). The Transportation Intermediaries Association (TIA) has separately cited a range of $500M–$700M in freight-payment losses attributable to freight fraud and double brokering (methodology not publicly disclosed), and by January 2025 revised that estimate upward to ‘$1 billion-plus.’ ATRI’s 2025 survey-extrapolation puts total direct and indirect industry costs at $1.8B–$6.6B. The original $500M–$700M range sits above Verisk’s directly measured 2023 figure ($332M) but below the 2024 measured figure ($455M) and below TIA’s own revised estimate; it appears to be a reasonable order-of-magnitude estimate for ~2022–2023, now likely understated for 2024–2025.

new_sources.key_figures: $454.9M estimated total cargo theft losses in 2024 (3,625 incidents, avg $202,364/incident); $331.9M in 2023; 27% YoY increase; fraud/deception methods rising to ~one-third of all incidents by 2024. Published January 21, 2025.
new_sources.supports: Partially supports the $500M–$700M range directionally but the measured figure for 2024 is $455M (below range). Confirms US+Canada scope and rising trend. Methodology: incident-based tracking via CargoNet platform, covering reported events.
new_sources.methodology_note: Incident-count × average-value methodology; known undercount due to voluntary reporting. Does NOT separate direct-fraud (identity theft, double brokering) from physical theft within the $455M total, though fraud-type incidents are a large and growing share.

new_sources.key_figures: $725M estimated total cargo theft losses in 2025 (60% increase from 2024’s $455M). Published January 22, 2026.
new_sources.supports: Confirms accelerating trend; 2025 figure now exceeds the original $500M–$700M claim range. Strengthens the claim as a reasonable near-term baseline for 2024–2025.

new_sources.publisher: Transportation Intermediaries Association (TIA) — industry association for freight brokers and 3PLs
new_sources.key_figures: Cites ‘$500 million to $700 million in freight payments annually’ attributable to freight fraud and double brokering. Source of underlying methodology not disclosed within document.
new_sources.supports: This is likely the primary origin of the $500M–$700M figure cited by Travelers and others. TIA cites it as an estimate without naming its own source. Tier 4 (industry association) not Tier 1–2 government/actuarial. Supports use of the figure as an industry-consensus estimate, not a government-measured statistic.

new_sources.key_figures: TIA revised its own estimate upward to ‘in excess of $1 billion’ annually by January 2025, indicating the $500M–$700M figure is now considered understated by TIA itself.
new_sources.supports: Confirms the $500M–$700M claim is no longer TIA’s current estimate. The claim should be updated to reflect the revised upward trajectory.

new_sources.publisher: American Transportation Research Institute (ATRI) — trucking industry research non-profit, ATA affiliate
new_sources.key_figures: Surveyed 95 for-hire carriers representing ~90,000 combination trucks; $16.2M in reported theft losses in 2023 across 555 incidents (avg $521K/carrier/year). Extrapolated industry-wide cost: $1.8B–$6.6B in direct and indirect costs. Note: this broader figure includes physical theft and indirect costs, not fraud-only.
new_sources.supports: Provides US-specific context. The broader $1.8B–$6.6B ATRI range is not directly comparable to the $500M–$700M direct-fraud-only claim; they measure different things. ATRI’s survey-based direct theft losses alone are much lower ($16M for the surveyed pool, extrapolated), but ATRI explicitly notes severe underreporting.

new_sources.publisher: Risk & Insurance (trade publication, citing Verisk CargoNet)
new_sources.key_figures: Confirms $454.9M in 2024 losses from Verisk CargoNet; $331.9M in 2023. 27% YoY increase. Quarterly breakdown provided.
new_sources.supports: Corroborating secondary source for the Verisk CargoNet figures.

new_sources.publisher: Fox Business (citing Verisk CargoNet VP Keith Lewis)
new_sources.key_figures: $454M combined US+Canada losses in 2024 (3,625 incidents). Fraud-related theft up 1,445% in the period tracked; traditional direct theft up ~20%. Published January 24, 2025.
new_sources.supports: Corroborates the Verisk figure and confirms the extraordinary growth rate of fraud-type theft within the total.

new_sources.publisher: National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB) — non-profit funded by insurance industry, closely tracks cargo crime
new_sources.key_figures: NICB confirmed cargo crime incidents rose 27% in 2024; expects 22% further increase in 2025. Does not publish its own aggregate dollar-loss figure independently of CargoNet data.
new_sources.supports: Corroborates incident growth trend; NICB does not publish a separate aggregate dollar-loss figure that would validate or contradict the $500M–$700M claim independently.

source_genealogy_note: The $500M–$700M figure’s provenance chain appears to be: TIA industry estimate (undisclosed methodology, circa 2022–2023) → picked up by Travelers Insurance marketing → widely cited in industry media. TIA itself does not disclose a primary source for this figure. By contrast, Verisk CargoNet’s incident-based actuarial tracking (Tier 3) directly measured $332M in 2023 and $455M in 2024 for all US+Canada cargo theft (physical + fraud combined). The fraud-only subset would be lower than these totals, but fraud as a share of incidents grew rapidly to ~one-third of all incidents by end-2024, and fraud-type thefts have disproportionately higher per-incident values. A reasonable fraud-only estimate for 2024 would be $150M–$225M (one-third of $455M) under conservative assumptions, or higher if fraud loads have above-average values. The $500M–$700M TIA figure likely includes broader freight-payment fraud (non-delivery of payment to legitimate carriers) beyond cargo theft measured by CargoNet, which would explain the gap.
recommendation_for_canonical_draft: REFINE with new sources. Replace the Travelers citation entirely. Use: ‘Cargo identity-theft and double-brokering fraud across the US and Canada resulted in an estimated $455M in measured losses in 2024 (Verisk CargoNet annual analysis, January 2025) — up 27% from $332M in 2023 — with fraud-type incidents (fictitious pickups, carrier identity theft, strategic theft) now comprising approximately one-third of all incidents. Industry-association estimates citing broader freight-payment fraud losses range from $500M–$700M (TIA, 2023 estimate, methodology not publicly disclosed) to “in excess of $1 billion” (TIA revised estimate, January 2025). For 2025, Verisk CargoNet estimated total losses of $725M (published January 2026).’ Tier should be upgraded to 3 (Verisk CargoNet) with TIA as Tier 4 corroboration. The $500M–$700M range is directionally defensible as a historical midpoint but should not be presented as a government-measured figure; it is an industry-association estimate. The canonical draft should cite Verisk CargoNet as primary and note TIA’s estimate as context.
